newsitem.title: USA: Senior Democratic senator backs US aid for Egypt.
newsitem.headline: Senior Democratic senator backs US aid for Egypt.

text.p: An influential Democratic senator on Friday praised Egypt's role in the Middle East peace process and urged that money for Cairo be restored to the annual U.S. foreign aid budget.

Sen. Robert Byrd, senior Democrat on the Appropriations Committee, said in a statement a subcommittee action to remove an earmarked $2.1 billion in military and economic assistance for Egypt was "flagrantly unfair."
"Egypt should be commended and rewarded for its diplomatic actions vis-a-vis the Palestinians and Israelis, not seemingly punished for her courage," the West Virginia senator said.

Byrd noted that Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak had assigned a key aide as an intermediary between Israelis and Palestinians and taken other steps to keep the two sides talking. "This Egyptian initiative, in fact, appears to be the only game in town," he said.
President Bill Clinton had requested the same level of aid for Egypt as has been provided for several years.

But the Senate Appropriations subcommittee on foreign operations on Wednesday removed the earmark for Egypt but agreed to provide Israel with $3.0 billion. Both countries have received the aid as part of U.S. support for the Camp David peace accords signed by Israel and Egypt in 1978.
The aid is part of an overall $13.2 billion U.S. foreign aid budget for the 1998 fiscal year, which starts Oct. 1.

Subcommittee chairman Sen. Mitch McConnell, Republican of Kentucky, was highly critical of Egypt's involvement in the peace process, charging that Mubarak had undercut negotiations on Jewish settlements in Hebron and taken the lead in suspending the multilateral peace talks.
His main criticism, however, concerned what he said were growing ties between Egypt and Libya, a country on the U.S. list of states that support terrorism.

Byrd said efforts would be made to revive the aid package when the full Appropriations Committee considered U.S. foreign aid legislation next week and, if necessary, when the full Senate voted on the bill later.

He said it was an insult to Egypt that the subcommitee agreed to provide $250 million for Jordan out of what was to be Egypt's aid account. While he did not dispute approval of the funds for Jordan, Byrd said the money should have come equally from the aid set aside for Egypt and Israel.

The State Department said on Thursday it stood by its request for aid to Egypt. The subcommittee's vote would not necessarily mean a cutoff of aid. The State Department would be free to provide aid to Cairo from the rest of the U.S. foreign aid budget.
As Byrd praised Mubarak, he criticised what he called "apparent flagging" of dedication to the peace process by the government of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

"It was just when there appeared to be hopeful momentum toward resolving the outstanding issues between Israel and her neighbours that the right wing in Israeli politics initiated settlement construction activities and pulled the rug out from under this momentum," Byrd said.
